wstep: This card describes the NCHFP Berry Syrup recipe made with raspberries, processed in a boiling-water bath.

akapity: NCHFP gives this recipe for juices of blueberries, cherries, grapes, raspberries (black or red) and strawberries, and says to use it only with the fruit listed.
Blackberries are not on the list, so this card covers only raspberries.
NCHFP uses 6½ cups of fresh or frozen fruit and 6¾ cups of sugar.
The recipe makes about 9 half-pint jars.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.
Wash fresh fruit, remove the stems and crush it in a saucepan.
Bring to a boil and simmer until soft, 5 to 10 minutes.
Strain hot through a colander and let it drain until cool enough to handle.
Strain the collected juice through a double layer of cheesecloth or a jelly bag and discard the dry pulp.
You should get about 4½ to 5 cups of juice.
Combine the juice with 6¾ cups of sugar in a large saucepan, bring to a boil and simmer for 1 minute.
For a syrup with whole fruit pieces, set aside 1 or 2 cups of the fresh or frozen fruit, combine them with the sugar and simmer as for regular syrup.
Remove from the heat, skim off the foam and fill clean half-pint or pint jars, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace.
Put on the lids and process in a boiling-water canner.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process half-pint and pint jars for 10 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process them for 15 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 20 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
The NCHFP table gives times only for half-pint and pint jars.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
